taxonomy.note: Kew accepts the species and two varieties. B010 keeps a species-level learner target while preserving the varietal structure; Hill Country material is strongly represented by var. pubescens.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Dalea compacta and both accepted varieties as native in Texas.
Barneby's treatment describes var. pubescens as widespread and locally abundant across the eastern Texas Hill Country.
Hays County — Barneby specimen 14503 is explicitly cited from Hays County under D. compacta var. pubescens.
Blanco County — Barneby specimen 14500 is explicitly cited from Blanco County.
Kerr County — Barneby specimen Heller 1857 is explicitly cited from Kerr County and the varietal distribution extends west to Kerr County.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Purola Preserve lists its local D. compacta occurrence as introduced at that particular site, so that site record is not used. The Hays evidence here comes from a separate herbarium specimen within Barneby's native Hill Country treatment.

morphology.look_here_first: Look for the combination of narrow linear leaflets and a dense swollen cylindrical-to-ovoid head; if the main question is D. compacta versus D. purpurea, move immediately to the calyx.
diagnostic_traits: herbaceous perennial forming clumps from a thick root/short caudex
leaves with few pairs of narrow linear to linear-elliptic leaflets
very dense terminal ovoid, oblong, or cylindrical/conelike flower heads
heads visibly swollen/compact compared with the loose-spiked D. enneandra
in var. pubescens leaflets are commonly less than 3 mm wide
strong D. purpurea separation is concentrated in calyx characters rather than flower color alone

confusers.separator: This is the priority confuser. Barneby treats the strongest differences as calyx characters: D. compacta has the larger calyx and characteristic external pubescence pattern; habit/foliage alone can be very similar.
Both make dense heads, but D. aurea is conspicuously silky/strigose in foliage and head; D. compacta emphasizes narrow linear leaflets and a swollen dense head.
D. enneandra has an elongated loose spike with flowers visibly separated; D. compacta packs them into a dense head.
